en.title: Telecommunications Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What telecommunications engineering covers, how degrees are organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What telecommunications engineering is
sections.text:
Telecommunications engineering is the design, building and operation of systems that carry information from one place to another. The information may be voice, data, video or control signals. The systems include radio links, copper cables, optical fibres, satellites, mobile networks, switching centres and the software that manages them.

The subject joins several fields. Mathematics and physics describe signals and electromagnetic waves. Circuit theory and electronics explain the hardware. Digital logic, microprocessors and programming explain the processing and control. Networks and traffic engineering explain how many users share one system.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace national regulations, equipment standards or a qualified engineer. Rules on licensing, spectrum, safety and professional registration differ by country. In Nigeria, for example, engineering registration is handled by COREN, the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria. Check the current official source for your country.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, a BEng in telecommunications or electrical/electronic engineering commonly takes about five years and includes industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnic students commonly take an ND, then supervised industrial work, then an HND. In the UK, a BEng commonly takes three years and an MEng four, with Scotland often one year longer. Ghana, Kenya and other countries have their own patterns.

The early years are usually shared with other engineering students: mathematics, physics, circuits and computing. Later years add communication systems, networks, radio and optical subjects, with laboratory work and a project. A master’s adds advanced theory and a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The course begins with tools: engineering mathematics, probability and statistics, physics of electricity and magnetism, circuit theory, electronic devices and amplifiers, digital logic, signals and systems, programming, and electrical measurements.

The core then moves to communication itself. Analogue systems cover modulation, noise and receivers. Digital systems cover sampling, quantisation, line codes and detection. Electromagnetic fields and waves lead to transmission lines, impedance matching, antennas and radio propagation. Microwave and radio-frequency engineering extends these ideas to high frequencies.

Digital signal processing and information theory support error-control coding. Data communications and networks, switching and traffic engineering explain how links become networks. Optical fibre, satellite and mobile communications are the main long-distance and access technologies. Microprocessors and embedded systems show how equipment is controlled.

Planning, management and security deal with real networks. Professional practice, ethics and regulation cover the engineer’s duties. Project management and technical reporting cover how work is planned and explained.

At master’s level come advanced digital communications, advanced wireless and propagation, optical networks and photonics, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work through calculations by hand and draw the system before writing equations. For a receiver, sketch the blocks and mark the signal and noise at each point. For a link, draw the transmitter, channel and receiver, and write the units on every line.

Learn the meaning of decibels, because most link budgets use them. Practise converting between watts, milliwatts and dBm. Check whether an answer is reasonable: a received power of many watts at a mobile phone is wrong.

Use simulation software after you understand the hand method, and test it on a simple case with a known answer. Treat laboratory work seriously. Measure, record and compare with theory, then explain any difference.

keyPoints: Telecommunications engineering designs and operates systems that carry voice, data and video.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Study the mathematical and circuit tools first, then communication systems, then networks.
Write units on every line and check that answers are physically reasonable.
Understand the hand method before you trust simulation software.
Professional registration and regulation differ by country; in Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering.

en.title: Engineering mathematics for telecommunications
en.short: Differentiation, integration, matrices, complex numbers, series, first-order equations and numerical methods.

sections.heading: Change and area
sections.text:
Differentiation gives the rate of change of a function; the derivative of tⁿ is ntⁿ⁻¹. The notation dy/dx means the derivative of y with respect to x. Integration reverses differentiation, and a definite integral gives signed area.

Example: if v = 3t² m/s, the distance from t = 0 to t = 2 s is ∫3t² dt = [t³] = 8 m. Check: the derivative of t³ is 3t².

sections.heading: Series and complex numbers
sections.text:
A sequence is an ordered list; a series is its sum. The geometric series a + ar + ar² + ... sums to a ÷ (1 − r) when |r| < 1. The ratio test helps decide whether a series converges.

Complex numbers have the form a + jb, where j² = −1; they represent magnitude and phase, useful for signals. Example: (3 + j4) has magnitude √(3² + 4²) = 5.

sections.heading: Matrices and equations
sections.text:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. Matrix methods solve linear systems such as two mesh currents. Matrices also transform vectors and represent networks.

First-order differential equations relate a quantity to its rate of change. The equation dy/dt + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 5 has solution y = 5e^(−2t). At t = 0.5 s, y = 5e^(−1) = 1.84 (to 3 s.f.). Check: e^(−1) = 0.3679, times 5 = 1.8395.

sections.heading: Numerical methods
sections.text: Numerical methods approximate answers when no exact formula is available. Euler’s method steps along a solution: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n). The trapezium rule approximates an integral by summing trapeziums. Newton-Raphson finds roots by x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n) ÷ f′(x_n). Always check convergence and step size.

keyPoints: Derivative of tⁿ is ntⁿ⁻¹; integration reverses differentiation.
A definite integral gives signed area under a curve.
Geometric series sum: a ÷ (1 − r) when |r| < 1.
Magnitude of a + jb is √(a² + b²).
First-order equation dy/dt + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 5 gives y = 5e^(−2t).
Euler’s method: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(t_n, y_n); Newton-Raphson: x_{n+1} = x_n − f(x_n) ÷ f′(x_n).

en.title: Probability and statistics for telecommunications
en.short: Random variables, distributions, expectation, sampling, estimation, testing and regression.

sections.heading: Random variables
sections.text: A random variable turns outcomes into numbers. It is discrete for counts, such as calls arriving per minute, and continuous for measurements, such as noise voltage. A discrete variable has a probability mass function P(X = x); a continuous one has a density f(x), and probability is the area under it. F(x) = P(X ≤ x) is the cumulative distribution.

sections.heading: Distributions, mean, variance
sections.text:
Common models: Bernoulli (one trial), binomial (successes in n trials), Poisson (rare events in time or space), exponential (waiting times) and normal or Gaussian (many small effects added). The expectation E[X] is the long-run mean: Σ x P(x), or ∫ x f(x) dx. The variance is Var(X) = E[(X − μ)²] = E[X²] − μ², where μ = E[X]; its square root is the standard deviation σ.

Example: Poisson traffic with mean λ = 3 calls per minute. P(X = 2) = e⁻³ × 3² ÷ 2! = 4.5 × 0.0498 ≈ 0.224. For a Poisson variable, E[X] = Var(X) = λ.

sections.heading: Sampling and estimation
sections.text:
A population is every possible measurement; a sample is the part you observe. In a simple random sample each item has an equal chance of selection. The sample mean x̄ estimates the population mean μ. The standard error of the mean is σ ÷ √n. With known σ, a 95% confidence interval is x̄ ± 1.96 σ ÷ √n.

Example: n = 100, x̄ = 50, σ = 10. Standard error = 10 ÷ 10 = 1, so the interval is 50 ± 1.96, that is 48.04 to 51.96.

sections.heading: Testing and regression
sections.text:
A hypothesis test sets a null hypothesis H₀ against an alternative. A test statistic is compared with a critical value, or a p-value with a significance level α. The p-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed if H₀ is true. A small p-value is evidence against H₀. The level α is the chance of rejecting a true H₀.

Linear regression fits y = a + bx by least squares, with b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)². It is used, for example, to relate measured noise power to temperature.

keyPoints: A random variable is discrete for counts and continuous for measurements.
Expectation E[X] = Σ x P(x) or ∫ x f(x) dx; variance Var(X) = E[X²] − μ².
For a Poisson variable with mean λ, E[X] = Var(X) = λ.
Standard error of the mean is σ ÷ √n; a 95% interval is x̄ ± 1.96 σ ÷ √n.
A small p-value is evidence against the null hypothesis; α is the chance of a false rejection.
Least-squares regression slope: b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)².

en.title: Physics: electricity and magnetism
en.short: Electric fields, potential, capacitance, DC, magnetism, induction, Maxwell’s equations and EM waves.

sections.heading: Electric fields and potential
sections.text:
An electric charge creates an electric field E, the force per unit positive charge: E = F ÷ q, in N/C or V/m. Field lines point from positive to negative charge.

Electric potential V is work per unit charge: V = W ÷ q, in volts. Potential difference is the work per unit charge between two points. In a uniform field, E = V ÷ d.

sections.heading: Capacitance
sections.text:
A capacitor stores separated charge. Capacitance is C = Q ÷ V, in farads (F). A parallel-plate capacitor has C = εA ÷ d, where A is plate area, d is separation and ε = ε0εr is permittivity. Stored energy is ½CV².

Example: A = 0.02 m², d = 1 mm = 0.001 m, εr = 2, ε0 = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
C = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 2 × 0.02 ÷ 0.001 = 3.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ F = 354 pF.
At V = 100 V, energy = ½ × 3.54 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 100² = 1.77 × 10⁻⁶ J.

sections.heading: Current and magnetism
sections.text:
Direct current (DC) is a steady flow of charge. Current is I = Q ÷ t, in amperes (A). A current creates a magnetic field B, measured in tesla (T). The field circles the conductor; the right-hand rule gives its direction.

A moving charge in a magnetic field feels F = qvB sinθ, where θ is the angle between velocity and field. The force is greatest when v and B are perpendicular.

sections.heading: Induction and EM waves
sections.text:
A changing magnetic flux Φ (field through an area) through a loop induces an emf (electromotive force): ε = −dΦ ÷ dt (Faraday’s law). Lenz’s law says the induced current opposes the change. Maxwell’s equations summarise electromagnetism: electric charges produce E; changing B produces E; currents and changing E produce B; there are no magnetic monopoles.

These rules allow electromagnetic waves: oscillating E and B fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel, travelling in vacuum at c = 1 ÷ √(μ0ε0) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. For a wave, c = fλ.

keyPoints: Electric field is force per unit positive charge, E = F ÷ q; potential is work per unit charge, V = W ÷ q.
Capacitance C = Q ÷ V; parallel-plate C = εA ÷ d; stored energy ½CV².
Direct current is steady charge flow, I = Q ÷ t; a current creates a magnetic field, and a moving charge feels F = qvB sinθ.
Faraday’s law: induced emf ε = −dΦ ÷ dt; Lenz’s law says the induced effect opposes the change.
Maxwell’s equations show changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other, giving electromagnetic waves.
In vacuum electromagnetic waves travel at c = 1 ÷ √(μ0ε0) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, with c = fλ.

en.title: Circuit theory: direct and alternating current
en.short: Ohm and Kirchhoff laws, network theorems, phasors, impedance, AC power, resonance and transients.

sections.heading: DC laws and theorems
sections.text:
Direct current (DC) flows one way. Ohm’s law: V = IR. Kirchhoff’s current law: currents into a node equal currents out. Kirchhoff’s voltage law: voltages around a closed loop sum to zero. Series resistors add; parallel resistances combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2.

Network theorems apply to linear circuits. Superposition adds responses to each independent source. Thevenin’s theorem replaces a network by a voltage source Vth in series with Rth; Norton’s uses a current source in parallel. Maximum power transfer occurs when load resistance equals source resistance.

sections.heading: Phasors and impedance
sections.text: Alternating current (AC) reverses periodically. A phasor is a complex number giving amplitude and phase at one frequency; RMS (root mean square) phasors are usual. Impedance Z = R + jX generalises resistance, with j = √−1. Reactance is X_L = ωL and X_C = −1/(ωC), where ω = 2πf. Series impedances add; parallel impedances combine by reciprocals. Inductor voltage leads current by 90°; capacitor current leads voltage by 90°.

sections.heading: AC power and resonance
sections.text:
AC power has real power P = VI cos φ, reactive power Q = VI sin φ and apparent power S = VI, using RMS values; cos φ is the power factor. Series resonance occurs when X_L and X_C cancel, so ω0 = 1/√(LC). Current is maximum and power factor unity.

Example: R = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH, C = 100 µF, V = 20 V RMS at ω0 = 1000 rad/s. X_L = 1000 × 0.01 = 10 Ω; X_C = −1 ÷ (1000 × 0.0001) = −10 Ω. They cancel, so Z = 10 Ω, I = 20 ÷ 10 = 2 A and P = I²R = 4 × 10 = 40 W.

sections.heading: First-order transients
sections.text: First-order transients arise when a capacitor or inductor changes stored energy. The time constant is τ = RC for a series RC circuit and τ = L/R for a series RL circuit. A capacitor charging from zero follows v_C = V(1 − e^(−t/τ)); an inductor current rising from zero follows i_L = I(1 − e^(−t/τ)). After about five time constants the change is almost complete.

keyPoints: Ohm’s law is V = IR; Kirchhoff’s laws conserve current at nodes and voltage around loops.
Superposition, Thevenin and Norton simplify linear circuits; maximum power transfer needs load resistance equal to source resistance.
Impedance is Z = R + jX, with X_L = ωL and X_C = −1/(ωC).
Real AC power is P = VI cos φ and apparent power is S = VI.
Series resonance gives ω0 = 1/√(LC), maximum current and unity power factor.
First-order time constants are τ = RC and τ = L/R; responses follow 1 − e^(−t/τ).

en.title: Electronic devices and amplifiers
en.short: Diodes, bipolar and field-effect transistors, biasing, small-signal amplifiers, op amps and feedback.

sections.heading: Diodes
sections.text:
A semiconductor diode is a pn junction. Forward bias, with the p side positive, narrows the depletion region and allows current above a threshold. Reverse bias blocks current, apart from small leakage.

A conducting silicon diode drops about 0.7 V; germanium about 0.3 V. These are typical values, not exact for every device. A series resistor limits current.

sections.heading: Transistors and biasing
sections.text:
A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has base, collector and emitter terminals. A small base current controls a larger collector current: IC ≈ βIB. β varies widely between devices.

A field-effect transistor (FET) is controlled by gate-source voltage; in a MOSFET the gate is insulated. Transconductance gm = ΔID ÷ ΔVGS. Biasing sets a steady direct-current operating point, the Q point, so the device stays active and the output can swing without clipping. Voltage-divider bias is common for BJTs; a source resistor sets an FET bias.

sections.heading: Small-signal amplifiers
sections.text:
A small-signal amplifier handles a small alternating signal around the Q point. The transistor is replaced by a linear model: a BJT by a controlled current source gm vbe, a FET by gm vgs. Voltage gain is output voltage divided by input voltage. For a common-emitter stage with collector resistor RC and the emitter resistor fully bypassed, gain magnitude ≈ gm RC = RC ÷ re, where re ≈ VT ÷ IE and VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.

Example: IE = 1 mA gives re = 26 Ω; with RC = 2.2 kΩ, gain magnitude ≈ 2200 ÷ 26 = 84.6. The negative sign means inversion.

sections.heading: Op amps and feedback
sections.text:
An operational amplifier is a high-gain differential amplifier. Negative feedback returns part of the output to the inverting input. It makes gain depend mainly on external resistors, not on the op amp’s open-loop gain.

For the non-inverting circuit, gain = 1 + Rf ÷ R1. For the inverting circuit, gain = −Rf ÷ R1. Feedback also widens bandwidth and reduces distortion, but too much can cause instability.

keyPoints: A silicon diode drops about 0.7 V in forward conduction; a germanium diode about 0.3 V.
For a BJT, IC ≈ βIB, and β varies between devices.
Biasing sets the Q point so the device stays active and the output can swing without clipping.
For a common-emitter stage, gain magnitude ≈ gm RC = RC ÷ re, with re ≈ VT ÷ IE and VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.
An op amp with negative feedback has gain 1 + Rf ÷ R1 when non-inverting and −Rf ÷ R1 when inverting.
Negative feedback trades open-loop gain for more predictable gain, wider bandwidth and less distortion.

en.title: Digital logic and number systems
en.short: Binary, hexadecimal, Boolean algebra, logic gates, flip-flops, counters and registers.

sections.heading: Number systems
sections.text:
Digital systems use two voltage bands, called logic levels, to represent 0 and 1. A binary number uses place values that double: for bits b_i, value = Σ b_i 2^i. Grouping four bits gives hexadecimal, which is compact for addresses and codes.

Example: 1011 0110₂ = 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182. In hexadecimal, 1011₂ = B and 0110₂ = 6, so the same number is B6₁₆ = 11 × 16 + 6 = 182. Decimal, octal and hexadecimal are just different bases for the same value.

sections.heading: Boolean algebra
sections.text:
Boolean algebra manipulates variables that take only 0 or 1. The main operations are AND (·), OR (+) and NOT (complement, written A′). Identities include A + 0 = A, A · 1 = A, A + A = A, A · A = A, A + A′ = 1 and A · A′ = 0. De Morgan’s laws are (A + B)′ = A′ · B′ and (A · B)′ = A′ + B′.

Simplification reduces gates. Example: A·B + A·B′ = A(B + B′) = A·1 = A. A truth table lists the output for every input combination; a Karnaugh map is a visual aid for simplification.

sections.heading: Combinational logic
sections.text: Combinational logic output depends only on the present inputs. Gates such as AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR are combined. A half adder adds two bits: sum = A ⊕ B and carry = A·B. A full adder adds A, B and a carry-in. Multiplexers select one of several inputs; decoders activate one output for each input code.

sections.heading: Sequential logic
sections.text: Sequential logic has memory. A flip-flop stores one bit and changes on a clock edge. The D flip-flop sets Q(next) = D. A register is several flip-flops sharing a clock, so an n-bit register stores n bits. A counter is a register that steps through states; an n-bit binary counter has 2ⁿ states. Logic levels and timing limits vary by logic family, so check the manufacturer’s datasheet.

keyPoints: Binary place value: value = Σ b_i 2^i; four bits form one hexadecimal digit.
De Morgan: (A + B)′ = A′ · B′ and (A · B)′ = A′ + B′.
Half adder: sum = A ⊕ B, carry = A·B.
A D flip-flop stores one bit with Q(next) = D.
An n-bit register stores n bits; an n-bit binary counter has 2ⁿ states.
Logic levels and timing limits depend on the logic family, so check the datasheet.

en.title: Signals and systems
en.short: Continuous and discrete signals, LTI systems, convolution, Fourier, Laplace and z transforms, and sampling.

sections.heading: Signals and systems
sections.text:
A signal is a function that carries information, such as a voltage. A continuous-time signal x(t) is defined for every t. A discrete-time signal x[n] is defined only at integer n, often from sampling. A system maps an input x to an output y.

A system is linear if superposition holds: a x1 + b x2 gives a y1 + b y2. It is time-invariant if a delayed input gives the same output delayed. A linear time-invariant (LTI) system is fully described by its impulse response h(t) or h[n], the output for a unit impulse.

sections.heading: LTI and convolution
sections.text:
Convolution gives the output of an LTI system:
y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ
y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n − k]
The output is a sum of scaled, shifted impulse responses. Convolution is commutative, associative and distributive.

Example: x[n] = [1, 2] and h[n] = [1, 1], starting at n = 0.
y[0] = 1×1 = 1
y[1] = 1×1 + 2×1 = 3
y[2] = 2×1 = 2
So y[n] = [1, 3, 2].

sections.heading: Transforms
sections.text:
The Fourier transform expresses a signal as sinusoids and shows its frequency content:
X(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(−j2πft) dt
The Laplace transform uses complex s = σ + jω:
X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(−st) dt
It handles transients and stability of continuous systems. The z transform is the discrete counterpart:
X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(−n)
It handles discrete systems and difference equations. Poles and zeros describe behaviour.

sections.heading: Sampling
sections.text: Sampling takes values of x(t) at intervals T, giving x[n] = x(nT) with sampling frequency fs = 1/T. Ideal sampling repeats the spectrum every fs. If x(t) is bandlimited to fmax and fs > 2fmax, the samples determine x(t) exactly. This is the Nyquist criterion; 2fmax is the Nyquist rate. If fs is too low, aliasing folds high frequencies onto low ones. An anti-alias filter before the sampler limits fmax.

keyPoints: A continuous-time signal is defined for all t; a discrete-time signal is defined at integer n.
An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response, and its output is the convolution y = x * h.
Fourier transform: X(f) = ∫ x(t) e^(−j2πft) dt; it gives the frequency content.
Laplace transform: X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(−st) dt with s = σ + jω; z transform: X(z) = Σ x[n] z^(−n).
Sampling at fs > 2fmax avoids aliasing and allows exact reconstruction of a bandlimited signal.
An anti-alias filter before the sampler limits the input bandwidth in practice.

en.title: Programming and computing tools
en.short: Variables, control flow, functions, arrays, files, and scripts for calculation, data handling and plotting signals.

sections.heading: Variables and control flow
sections.text: In a general-purpose language such as Python, a program stores data in variables. A variable is a named place in memory that holds a value, such as an integer, a floating-point number, a string or a Boolean. Assignment gives it a new value. Control flow sets the order in which statements run. An if statement chooses between branches. A for loop repeats over a sequence, such as array items. A while loop repeats while a condition remains true. These structures let one script handle many samples without repeating lines by hand.

sections.heading: Functions and arrays
sections.text: A function is a named block of code that takes inputs, called parameters, and returns a result. Functions avoid repetition and make testing easier. An array stores many values under one name. Each value is reached by an index, which usually starts at zero in Python and many other languages. Arrays hold sampled data, filter coefficients or table columns. Whole-array operations are often faster and clearer than element-by-element loops.

sections.heading: Files and scripts
sections.text: A script is a file of commands run in order. It can read a text or CSV (comma-separated values) file, convert lines to numbers, store them in arrays, calculate results and write a summary file. Close a file after use, or use a language feature that closes it automatically. A plotting library draws one array against another. For a signal, plot sample values against time and label both axes with units.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text:
Example:
samples = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
total = 0
for x in samples:
    total = total + x
mean = total / 4
print(mean)
The output is 2.5, because 1.0 + 2.0 + 3.0 + 4.0 = 10.0 and 10.0 ÷ 4 = 2.5.

To plot a signal:
t = [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75]
y = [0, 1, 0, -1]
plot(t, y)
The four points are drawn against time in seconds. Check units and sample spacing before trusting a plot.

keyPoints: Variables name stored values; control flow decides which statements run and how often.
Functions take parameters and return results, which makes code reusable and testable.
Arrays store many values under one name; each value is reached by an index, usually starting at zero.
Scripts read files, calculate results and write output in a repeatable order.
Plot signal samples against time and always label axes with units.
The mean is the sum of samples divided by the number of samples; check arithmetic by hand.

en.title: Electrical measurements and instruments
en.short: Units, errors, analogue and digital meters, oscilloscope, signal generator, frequency counter and spectrum analyser.

sections.heading: Units and errors
sections.text:
Measurement gives a quantity as a number times a unit. The SI base electrical unit is the ampere; the volt, ohm and watt are derived units. Prefixes such as milli (10⁻³), kilo (10³) and mega (10⁶) scale values.

No measurement is exact. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability. Systematic errors shift every reading the same way, such as a zero offset. Random errors scatter and fall when readings are averaged. Resolution is the smallest change an instrument can show.

Absolute error = measured value − true value. Percentage error = (absolute error ÷ true value) × 100%. If a 100.0 Ω resistor reads 101.5 Ω, the error is +1.5 Ω, or +1.5%.

sections.heading: Analogue and digital meters
sections.text:
Analogue meters move a pointer. A moving-coil meter responds to average direct current; a moving-iron meter can respond to alternating current. They are simple but suffer parallax and limited resolution.

Digital meters use an analogue-to-digital converter and show digits. A digital multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance. Its resolution is the least significant digit; accuracy is quoted as a tolerance, often a percentage plus a few counts. A voltmeter should have high resistance and an ammeter very low resistance, so the meter disturbs the circuit as little as possible.

sections.heading: Oscilloscope and generator
sections.text:
An oscilloscope displays voltage against time. The vertical control sets volts per division; the timebase sets seconds per division. A probe connects the signal, and triggering stabilises the display. Peak-to-peak voltage = vertical divisions × volts per division. Period = horizontal divisions × time per division; frequency = 1 ÷ period.

A signal generator produces test waveforms, usually sine, square or triangle, with adjustable frequency and amplitude.

sections.heading: Frequency and spectrum
sections.text: A frequency counter counts cycles N in a gate time t: f = N ÷ t. If N = 2,500 in 0.1 s, f = 25,000 Hz. A spectrum analyser plots signal amplitude against frequency. It is often used for radio-frequency signals and shows harmonics and interference.

keyPoints: Percentage error = (measured value − true value) ÷ true value × 100%.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability.
A voltmeter needs high resistance and an ammeter very low resistance.
Oscilloscope: peak-to-peak voltage = vertical divisions × volts per division; frequency = 1 ÷ period.
Frequency counter: f = N ÷ t, where N is the counted cycles and t is the gate time.
A spectrum analyser displays amplitude against frequency; it is often used for radio-frequency signals.

en.title: Analogue communication systems
en.short: Amplitude and angle modulation, modulators and demodulators, receivers, bandwidth, noise and SNR.

sections.heading: Amplitude modulation
sections.text:
In amplitude modulation (AM) the message changes the carrier amplitude: s(t) = Ac[1 + m cos(2πfmt)] cos(2πfct), where m = Am ÷ Ac is the modulation index. For m ≤ 1 the envelope follows the message.

Full-carrier AM needs bandwidth 2fm. Double-sideband suppressed carrier (DSB-SC) also needs 2fm; single-sideband (SSB) needs fm. Overmodulation (m > 1) distorts the envelope.

sections.heading: Angle modulation
sections.text:
In frequency modulation (FM) the message changes the carrier frequency. The frequency deviation is Δf = kf Am, and the modulation index is β = Δf ÷ fm. Phase modulation (PM) changes carrier phase instead.

FM and PM have constant envelope, so they resist amplitude noise, but need more bandwidth. Carson’s rule estimates FM bandwidth as B ≈ 2(Δf + fm). Small β gives narrowband FM; large β gives wideband FM.

sections.heading: Modulators and receivers
sections.text:
AM is generated by multiplying the carrier by the message plus a DC bias; a switching modulator uses a diode. FM is often generated by a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO). Demodulation uses an envelope detector for AM, a coherent detector for DSB-SC and SSB, and a discriminator or phase-locked loop (PLL) for FM.

Most receivers are superheterodyne: RF stage, mixer with local oscillator, intermediate-frequency (IF) amplifier for selectivity, then detector. The image frequency is fs + 2fIF when the local oscillator runs above the signal.

sections.heading: Noise and SNR
sections.text:
The available thermal noise power is N = kTB, where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T is absolute temperature and B is noise bandwidth. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is signal power ÷ noise power. Noise figure F = SNRin ÷ SNRout compares a receiver with an ideal one; NF = 10 log10 F in dB.

Wider bandwidth admits more noise, so FM trades bandwidth for better SNR above a threshold. Example: N = 1.38 × 10^-23 × 290 × 10^4 = 4.00 × 10^-17 W at 290 K and 10 kHz. A 1 pW signal gives SNR = 1 × 10^-12 ÷ 4.00 × 10^-17 = 2.50 × 10^4 = 44.0 dB.

keyPoints: AM modulation index is m = Am ÷ Ac; m ≤ 1 avoids envelope distortion.
Full-carrier AM and DSB-SC need bandwidth 2fm; SSB needs fm.
FM modulation index is β = Δf ÷ fm, and Carson’s rule gives B ≈ 2(Δf + fm).
Envelope detection suits AM; coherent detection suits DSB-SC and SSB; FM uses a discriminator or PLL.
A superheterodyne receiver uses a fixed IF for selectivity; image frequency is fs + 2fIF for high-side injection.
Thermal noise power is N = kTB, SNR = signal power ÷ noise power, and noise figure F = SNRin ÷ SNRout.

en.title: Digital communication systems
en.short: Sampling, quantisation, PCM, line codes, ASK/FSK/PSK/QAM, detection, BER and eye diagrams.

sections.heading: Sampling and quantisation
sections.text:
Sampling turns a continuous signal into discrete-time samples. The Nyquist criterion says the rate must be at least twice the highest frequency, fs ≥ 2B, or aliasing folds high frequencies onto low ones. An anti-alias filter limits B.

Quantisation rounds each sample to one of 2^n levels. The step is Δ. If error is uniform noise, its power is Δ²/12. For a full-scale sine, the signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio (SQNR) is about 6.02n + 1.76 dB. Example: n = 8 gives 6.02 × 8 + 1.76 = 49.9 dB.

sections.heading: PCM and line codes
sections.text:
Pulse-code modulation (PCM) samples, quantises and encodes each sample as n bits. Bit rate R = n fs. Example: telephone voice sampled at 8 kHz with 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s. Companding (A-law or mu-law) gives small signals more levels; the choice is a standard, not a law of physics.

Line codes shape bits for the cable. NRZ holds the level for a whole bit, RZ returns to zero, Manchester has a transition every bit for clock recovery, and AMI alternates polarity to remove DC.

sections.heading: Digital modulation
sections.text: Digital modulation maps bits onto a carrier. ASK varies amplitude, FSK varies frequency, PSK varies phase, and QAM varies amplitude and phase together. With M symbols each symbol carries log2 M bits. BPSK and QPSK are robust; 16-QAM carries 4 bits per symbol but needs a higher signal-to-noise ratio for the same error rate.

sections.heading: Detection, BER and eye diagrams
sections.text:
Detection decides which symbol arrived. A coherent receiver uses the carrier phase and a matched filter, which maximises SNR at the sampling instant; a noncoherent receiver does not need phase. For BPSK in additive white Gaussian noise, the bit-error rate is Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)), where Eb/N0 is energy per bit over noise density and Q is the Gaussian tail function. BER falls steeply as Eb/N0 rises.

An eye diagram overlays many symbol intervals. An open eye means good noise margin; closure shows intersymbol interference, noise or timing jitter.

keyPoints: Sampling rate must satisfy fs ≥ 2B to avoid aliasing.
Uniform quantisation noise power is Δ²/12; full-scale sine SQNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB.
PCM bit rate is R = n fs; 8 kHz at 8 bits gives 64 kbit/s.
M-ary modulation carries log2 M bits per symbol.
BPSK bit-error rate in AWGN is Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)).
An eye diagram shows noise margin, intersymbol interference and timing jitter.

en.title: Electromagnetic fields and waves
en.short: Maxwell’s equations, plane waves, polarisation, reflection, power flow and guided waves.

sections.heading: Maxwell to wave equation
sections.text:
Maxwell’s four equations relate electric field E, magnetic flux density B, charge and current. Gauss’s law for electricity says charge is the source of E. Gauss’s law for magnetism says there are no magnetic monopoles. Faraday’s law says a changing B induces a circulating E. The Ampere-Maxwell law says current and a changing E induce a circulating B.

In a source-free region they combine into the wave equation. For a plane wave varying along z: d²E/dz² = μ0 ε0 d²E/dt². The speed is c = 1/√(μ0 ε0) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum. In a lossless medium use μ and ε: v = 1/√(με) and n = c/v.

sections.heading: Plane waves and polarisation
sections.text:
A uniform plane wave has E and H constant over planes perpendicular to the direction of travel. E, H and that direction are mutually perpendicular, so the wave is transverse electromagnetic (TEM). In a lossless medium H = E/η, where η = √(μ/ε) is the intrinsic impedance; free space has η0 ≈ 377 Ω.

Polarisation is the path traced by the tip of E. It is linear if E stays along one line, circular if two equal perpendicular components are 90° out of phase, and elliptical otherwise.

sections.heading: Reflection, refraction, power
sections.text:
At a flat boundary, Snell’s law gives n1 sin θi = n2 sin θt. The Fresnel equations give reflected and transmitted amplitudes; they differ for polarisation parallel and perpendicular to the plane of incidence. When n1 > n2 and θi exceeds the critical angle θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1), total internal reflection occurs.

The Poynting vector S = E × H is power flow per unit area. For a plane wave the time-average is S = E0²/(2η). Example: E0 = 10 V/m in free space gives S = 10²/(2 × 377) = 0.133 W/m².

sections.heading: Guided waves
sections.text: Guided waves are confined by conductors or dielectrics. Two-conductor lines support TEM waves. Hollow waveguides support TE or TM modes only above a cutoff frequency; below it the wave decays.

keyPoints: Maxwell’s four equations relate E, B, charge and current, and in a source-free region they give the wave equation.
Plane-wave speed is c = 1/√(μ0 ε0) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum, and v = 1/√(με) in a lossless medium.
In a lossless plane wave E and H are perpendicular, H = E/η with η = √(μ/ε), and free space has η0 ≈ 377 Ω.
Polarisation is linear, circular or elliptical according to the components of E.
Snell’s law n1 sin θi = n2 sin θt and the Fresnel equations describe reflection and refraction, while total internal reflection needs n1 > n2 and θi > θc.
The Poynting vector S = E × H gives power density, with time-average E0²/(2η) for a plane wave, while guided waves are TEM on two-conductor lines or TE/TM above cutoff in hollow waveguides.

en.title: Transmission lines and impedance matching
en.short: Distributed lines, characteristic impedance, reflection, VSWR, Smith chart and stub or quarter-wave matching.

sections.heading: Distributed model
sections.text:
At high frequency a line is a distributed circuit: series inductance L and shunt capacitance C per metre, plus loss terms. For a lossless line, characteristic impedance Z0 = √(L/C) and wave velocity v = 1/√(LC). Z0 is the voltage-to-current ratio of one travelling wave, not the load.

A line of length l terminated by ZL has Zin = Z0 (ZL + jZ0 tan βl) ÷ (Z0 + jZL tan βl), with β = 2π/λ. If ZL = Z0 there is no reflection.

sections.heading: Reflection and VSWR
sections.text:
Reflection coefficient Γ = (ZL − Z0) ÷ (ZL + Z0). Its magnitude gives the reflected voltage fraction; its angle gives phase. VSWR (voltage standing wave ratio) = (1 + |Γ|) ÷ (1 − |Γ|). A matched load has Γ = 0 and VSWR = 1.

Example: Z0 = 50 Ω, ZL = 100 Ω.
Γ = (100 − 50) ÷ (100 + 50) = 0.333
VSWR = (1 + 0.333) ÷ (1 − 0.333) = 2.0
Reflected power fraction = |Γ|² = 0.111, about 11%.

sections.heading: Smith chart
sections.text:
The Smith chart plots normalized impedance z = Z ÷ Z0 as reflection coefficient. Constant resistance circles and reactance arcs all pass through the open-circuit point Γ = 1; the centre Γ = 0 is the matched point z = 1.

Moving toward the generator along a lossless line rotates the point clockwise by 2βl. It gives Γ, VSWR, impedance and admittance graphically, and is used to design matching.

sections.heading: Matching methods
sections.text:
Quarter-wave matching uses a λ/4 section of impedance Z1 = √(Z0 ZL) between feed line and a real load, since its input impedance is Z1² ÷ ZL. For 50 Ω feeding 100 Ω, Z1 = √(50 × 100) = 70.7 Ω. It is narrowband and needs a real load.

Stub matching places a short or open stub a distance d from the load; d is chosen so the admittance looking toward the load has conductance Y0 = 1/Z0, and the stub cancels the remaining susceptance. Stub length and d come from the Smith chart or calculation. Both transform the load to Z0, lowering reflection and VSWR.

keyPoints: For a lossless line, Z0 = √(L/C) and v = 1/√(LC).
Reflection coefficient: Γ = (ZL − Z0) ÷ (ZL + Z0).
VSWR = (1 + |Γ|) ÷ (1 − |Γ|); a matched load gives VSWR = 1.
A quarter-wave transformer matches a real load with Z1 = √(Z0 ZL) and is narrowband.
Stub matching: d is chosen so the admittance looking toward the load has conductance Y0, and the stub cancels the remaining susceptance.
On the Smith chart, moving toward the generator moves the impedance point clockwise by 2βl.

en.title: Antennas and radio propagation
en.short: Antenna gain, radiation patterns, dipoles, arrays, Friis, link budgets and propagation mechanisms.

sections.heading: Gain and patterns
sections.text: An antenna converts a guided wave into a radiated wave. Directivity D compares the strongest power density with the average over all directions. Gain G = ηD includes efficiency η, so gain is never greater than directivity. Both are quoted in dBi: dBi = 10 log10 G relative to an isotropic radiator (D = 1). A radiation pattern plots power or field against angle, showing the main lobe, side lobes and half-power beamwidth, where power falls to half its peak.

sections.heading: Dipoles and arrays
sections.text: A half-wave dipole is about λ/2 long. Its directivity is 1.64, or 2.15 dBi; its feed impedance in free space is near 73 Ω, with some reactance unless adjusted for resonance. An array feeds several elements with controlled phase. Its total pattern is the element pattern multiplied by the array factor. A broadside array has maxima at right angles to its axis; an end-fire array has maxima along the axis. Spacing and phase set beam direction and side-lobe level.

sections.heading: Friis and link budget
sections.text: For line-of-sight, far-field links, Friis gives received power: Pr = Pt Gt Gr (λ ÷ (4πd))². Path loss is L = (4πd ÷ λ)². In decibels: Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − 20 log10(4πd ÷ λ). A link budget adds gains and subtracts losses. Example: Pt = 20 dBm, Gt = 10 dBi, Gr = 2 dBi, f = 2.4 GHz, d = 1 km. λ = 0.125 m. Path loss = 20 log10(4π × 1000 ÷ 0.125) = 100.05 dB. Pr = 20 + 10 + 2 − 100.05 = −68.05 dBm.

sections.heading: Propagation mechanisms
sections.text: Radio waves arrive by several mechanisms. Free-space propagation is direct line of sight. Reflection comes from ground and buildings; diffraction bends waves around edges; scattering spreads energy from rough surfaces and rain; absorption by gases and rain adds loss. At HF, skywave reflection from the ionosphere matters; at VHF and above, terrain and tropospheric effects dominate. Multipath causes fading, so link budgets include a fade margin.

keyPoints: Directivity compares peak radiation to the average; gain is G = ηD and is quoted in dBi.
A half-wave dipole has directivity 1.64 (2.15 dBi) and input impedance near 73 Ω in free space.
Array pattern equals element pattern times array factor; phase and spacing steer the beam.
Friis for line-of-sight far-field links: Pr = Pt Gt Gr (λ ÷ (4πd))².
Link budget in dB: Pr = Pt + Gt + Gr − 20 log10(4πd ÷ λ) − other losses − margins.
Propagation includes free-space, reflection, diffraction, scattering and absorption; multipath causes fading.

en.title: Microwave and radio-frequency engineering
en.short: Waveguides, S-parameters, microwave components, filters, oscillators and basic RF measurement.

sections.heading: Waveguides
sections.text: At microwave frequencies, ordinary two-wire lines radiate and lose power. A waveguide is a hollow metal pipe that guides the wave inside. Its size sets a cutoff frequency below which the wave cannot propagate. For an air-filled rectangular guide in the dominant TE10 mode, fc = c ÷ (2a), where a is the broad inside width. Example: a = 22.86 mm gives fc = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ (2 × 0.02286) = 6.56 GHz. Above cutoff, loss is low but bandwidth is limited.

sections.heading: S-parameters and components
sections.text:
Scattering parameters describe a network by waves, not voltages and currents. At a port, a is the incident wave and b is the reflected or transmitted wave. S11 = b1 ÷ a1 with port 2 matched; S21 = b2 ÷ a1. Insertion loss in dB is −20 log10 |S21|. Example: |S21| = 0.5 gives −20 log10 0.5 = 6.02 dB.

Passive components include couplers, dividers, isolators, circulators and attenuators. Active components, such as low-noise amplifiers and power amplifiers, need DC bias and can add gain.

sections.heading: Filters and oscillators
sections.text:
Filters pass wanted frequencies and reject others: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop. Key terms are passband, stopband, cutoff, insertion loss and return loss. They can use distributed elements, such as stubs on a microstrip line, or lumped inductors and capacitors at lower RF.

An oscillator turns DC power into a periodic RF signal using positive feedback and a resonant circuit. Important properties are frequency, tuning range, output power, stability and phase noise, the short-term random variation of frequency. A voltage-controlled oscillator tunes frequency with a control voltage.

sections.heading: Measurement
sections.text: Basic microwave measurement uses a vector network analyser (VNA) for S-parameters, a power meter for absolute power and a spectrum analyser for frequency and phase noise. The VNA is calibrated with known standards, often short, open, load and thru. Results should be traceable to a national metrology institute; accreditation and calibration rules differ by country, so check the current official requirements.

keyPoints: Rectangular waveguide dominant-mode cutoff: fc = c ÷ (2a).
S11 and S21 are ratios of wave amplitudes with matched ports.
Insertion loss in dB = −20 log10 |S21|.
Filters are described by passband, stopband, cutoff, insertion loss and return loss.
Oscillator quality includes frequency stability, tuning range, output power and phase noise.
A vector network analyser measures S-parameters after calibration with known standards.

en.title: Digital signal processing
en.short: Discrete-time signals, DFT and FFT, FIR and IIR filters, spectral analysis and telecom uses.

sections.heading: Discrete-time signals
sections.text: A discrete-time signal is a sequence x[n] defined at integer instants n. It comes from sampling a continuous signal at rate fs, so n corresponds to time n/fs. The unit impulse δ[n] is 1 at n = 0 and 0 elsewhere; any sequence can be written as a sum of scaled, shifted impulses. Systems are described by difference equations, such as y[n] = 0.5y[n−1] + x[n]. The z-transform generalises the Fourier transform for stability and design work.

sections.heading: DFT and FFT
sections.text:
The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) maps N samples to N frequency bins: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N), n = 0 to N − 1. Bin k is at frequency k fs/N. The fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes the same result with about N log₂ N operations instead of N².

Example: x = [1, 0, 1, 0], N = 4. X[0] = 1 + 1 = 2. X[1] = 1 + e^(−jπ) = 0. X[2] = 1 + e^(−j2π) = 2. X[3] = 1 + e^(−j3π) = 0. The non-zero bins are at 0 and fs/2.

sections.heading: FIR and IIR filters
sections.text: An FIR filter has a finite impulse response: y[n] = Σ b_k x[n−k]. It is always stable when the coefficients are finite, and it can be designed for exact linear phase, which means constant delay. An IIR filter uses feedback: y[n] = Σ b_k x[n−k] − Σ a_k y[n−k]. It can meet a specification with a lower order, but it may be unstable and its phase is usually non-linear. Common FIR design uses windows; common IIR design uses the bilinear transform, which converts an analog filter design into a digital IIR filter.

sections.heading: Spectral analysis and applications
sections.text: Spectral analysis estimates how signal power is spread over frequency. A finite record causes leakage, so a window such as Hamming is applied before the DFT. Resolution is about fs/N; zero-padding interpolates the spectrum but does not improve true resolution. In telecommunications, DSP performs channel filtering, equalisation, modulation and demodulation, spectrum monitoring and echo cancellation.

keyPoints: DFT: X[k] = Σ x[n] e^(−j2πkn/N) for n = 0 to N − 1.
FFT computes the DFT in about N log₂ N operations instead of N².
FIR: y[n] = Σ b_k x[n−k]; finite coefficients give guaranteed stability.
IIR: y[n] = Σ b_k x[n−k] − Σ a_k y[n−k]; check stability because feedback can oscillate.
DFT bin spacing is fs/N, so longer records give finer frequency resolution.
Windowing reduces leakage before spectral analysis.

en.title: Information theory and error-control coding
en.short: Entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, source coding, block and convolutional codes and ARQ.

sections.heading: Entropy and information
sections.text: Entropy measures the average uncertainty of a random source. For a discrete source with symbol probabilities p_i, H(X) = −Σ p_i log2 p_i bits per symbol. A fair coin has H = 1 bit; a certain symbol has H = 0. Mutual information I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) is the reduction in uncertainty about X after observing Y. It is symmetric and non-negative.

sections.heading: Channel capacity
sections.text: Channel capacity C is the largest mutual information between input and output, in bits per channel use: C = max I(X;Y). For a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, C = 1 − H2(p), where H2(p) = −p log2 p − (1−p) log2(1−p). Example: p = 0.1 gives H2(0.1) ≈ 0.469, so C ≈ 0.531 bit per use. Reliable communication is possible at rates below C, not above it.

sections.heading: Source coding
sections.text: Source coding removes redundancy before transmission. The Shannon source coding theorem says the average code length cannot be less than the source entropy H. Huffman coding builds a prefix code, so no codeword is the start of another, and gives the shortest average length for a known symbol distribution. Example: symbols with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.125 have H = 1.75 bits; Huffman lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 give average 1.75 bits, meeting the bound.

sections.heading: Error control
sections.text: Error-control coding adds redundant bits so the receiver can detect or correct errors. A block code (n,k) carries k data bits in n coded bits; rate = k/n. Minimum Hamming distance d_min detects d_min − 1 errors and corrects floor((d_min − 1)/2). Convolutional codes encode a continuous bit stream using a shift register; constraint length and rate describe them, and Viterbi decoding finds the most likely path. Automatic repeat request (ARQ) uses an error-detecting code such as a CRC: the receiver asks for retransmission after detected errors. Stop-and-wait, go-back-N and selective repeat are common ARQ schemes.

keyPoints: Entropy is H(X) = −Σ p_i log2 p_i bits per symbol.
Mutual information is I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y).
Channel capacity is C = max I(X;Y); for a binary symmetric channel C = 1 − H2(p).
Source coding cannot beat the entropy bound on average code length.
An (n,k) block code has rate k/n and corrects floor((d_min − 1)/2) errors.
ARQ detects errors and requests retransmission; common schemes are stop-and-wait, go-back-N and selective repeat.

en.title: Data communications and networks
en.short: OSI and TCP/IP models, Ethernet, IP addressing and routing, transport protocols, LANs, WANs and internet operation.

sections.heading: Layered models
sections.text: Layered models divide network tasks so each layer serves the one above. The OSI reference model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. The TCP/IP model used on the internet is usually described with four: link, internet, transport and application. OSI is a teaching reference; TCP/IP is the working suite. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for exchanging messages, and a service is what one layer offers to the layer above.

sections.heading: Ethernet and LANs
sections.text: Ethernet is the dominant local area network (LAN) technology. It sends frames, which carry source and destination MAC addresses, over a shared or switched link. A switch learns which MAC address is on each port and forwards frames only where needed, reducing collisions. A LAN covers a limited site. A wide area network (WAN) connects sites across towns or countries, often through a carrier. The internet is a network of networks that uses TCP/IP and exchanges routes between autonomous systems (networks run by a single operator).

sections.heading: IP addressing and routing
sections.text: An IP address identifies an interface. IPv4 uses 32 bits, written as four decimal octets; IPv6 uses 128 bits. A prefix length gives the network part: /24 means 24 network bits. Routing sends a packet towards its destination by matching the longest prefix in a routing table. A router connects different networks. Example: 192.168.10.130/26. A /26 has 2^(32−26) = 64 addresses. The block starts at 192.168.10.128, so usable host addresses run from 192.168.10.129 to 192.168.10.190, with 192.168.10.191 as broadcast.

sections.heading: Transport and internet
sections.text: Transport protocols provide end-to-end delivery. TCP sets up a connection, numbers bytes, acknowledges data and retransmits lost segments, so it gives reliable, ordered delivery. UDP sends datagrams without a connection or delivery guarantee, which suits short or delay-sensitive traffic. Port numbers identify applications. Domain names are resolved to IP addresses by DNS, and web pages are commonly fetched with HTTP over TCP. These application protocols run above transport; the lower layers move bits and frames.

keyPoints: OSI has seven layers; the TCP/IP suite is usually described with four.
Ethernet frames use MAC addresses, and switches forward frames by learned MAC address.
For an ordinary IPv4 host subnet, a /n prefix contains 2^(32−n) addresses and 2^(32−n)−2 usable host addresses.
Routers choose the longest matching prefix in the routing table.
TCP gives reliable ordered delivery; UDP gives connectionless datagram delivery.
DNS maps names to IP addresses, and the internet interconnects autonomous systems using TCP/IP.

en.title: Switching systems and traffic engineering
en.short: Circuit and packet switching, PSTN signalling, traffic intensity in erlangs, blocking and simple queues.

sections.heading: Circuit and packet switching
sections.text:
Circuit switching sets up a dedicated path before data flows. Capacity is reserved on every link for the whole call, so delay is fixed and no queueing occurs once the call is accepted. If no route has a free circuit, the call is blocked.

Packet switching breaks a message into packets. Each packet carries an address and is forwarded independently, store and forward. Links are shared statistically, so capacity is used better, but packets queue and may be delayed or lost.

sections.heading: PSTN and signalling
sections.text:
The public switched telephone network (PSTN) is hierarchical. Subscriber lines reach a local exchange; trunk routes connect local, tandem and international gateway exchanges.

Signalling carries call control: address digits, ringing, answer and release. Common-channel signalling such as SS7 sends these messages on a separate packet network instead of inside each voice channel, which speeds up call setup.

sections.heading: Traffic intensity
sections.text:
Traffic intensity A measures how much a resource is occupied. It is dimensionless and quoted in erlangs. If calls arrive at λ per hour and each holds a circuit for a mean of h hours, then A = λ × h.

Example: 120 calls per hour with mean holding time 3 minutes = 0.05 hour. A = 120 × 0.05 = 6 erlang. That is the average number of circuits busy; design needs spare capacity above it.

sections.heading: Blocking and queues
sections.text:
Blocking probability B is the chance a call finds every circuit busy. For a loss system of N circuits offered traffic A, Erlang B gives B = (A^N ÷ N!) ÷ Σ(A^k ÷ k!), for k = 0 to N. Blocked calls are cleared, not queued.

M/M/1 means Poisson arrivals, exponential service and one server. With arrival rate λ and service rate μ, utilisation is ρ = λ ÷ μ, and the model is stable only if ρ < 1. Mean time in the system is W = 1 ÷ (μ − λ).

keyPoints: Circuit switching reserves a dedicated path and blocks a call when no route has free capacity.
Packet switching shares links statistically, so packets may queue, be delayed or be lost.
Traffic intensity A = λ × h, measured in erlangs, where h is mean holding time in hours.
Erlang B gives blocking probability for a loss system of N circuits carrying offered traffic A.
For M/M/1, utilisation ρ = λ ÷ μ and the queue is stable only when ρ < 1.
Mean time in an M/M/1 system is W = 1 ÷ (μ − λ).

en.title: Optical fibre communications
en.short: Fibre structure and modes, attenuation and dispersion, sources and detectors, WDM and link budgets.

sections.heading: Fibre structure and modes
sections.text: An optical fibre guides light in a core of slightly higher refractive index n1 than the cladding n2 around it. Total internal reflection keeps light in the core. Step-index fibre has a sharp index step; graded-index fibre has a gradual profile that reduces modal dispersion. Multimode fibre carries many paths and suits short links. Single-mode fibre carries one mode and suits long haul. For step-index fibre, numerical aperture NA = √(n1² − n2²) and V = 2πaNA/λ, where a is core radius and λ wavelength. Single-mode operation needs V below 2.405.

sections.heading: Attenuation and dispersion
sections.text: Attenuation is quoted in dB/km. Total loss in dB is 10 log10(Pin/Pout). Fibre has low-loss windows near 850, 1300 and 1550 nm; 1550 nm is usually lowest for long haul. Dispersion spreads pulses and limits bit rate times distance. Modal dispersion comes from different paths in multimode fibre. Chromatic dispersion comes from source linewidth and material/waveguide effects, quoted in ps/(nm·km). Single-mode fibre removes modal dispersion but still has chromatic and polarisation-mode dispersion.

sections.heading: Sources and detectors
sections.text: Sources are light-emitting diodes (LEDs) for short multimode links and semiconductor lasers for long single-mode links. Lasers give narrow linewidth and higher power but cost more. Detectors are PIN photodiodes and avalanche photodiodes (APDs). Responsivity, in A/W, converts optical power to current. APDs multiply current but add noise.

sections.heading: WDM and link budget
sections.text:
Wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) sends several wavelengths through one fibre. A multiplexer combines them and a demultiplexer separates them; erbium-doped fibre amplifiers (EDFAs) amplify bands without electronic regeneration. A link budget compares available power with losses. Budget = Pt − Pr(min). Losses = fibre loss × length + connector and splice losses + margin. Use datasheet values. Check national standards.
Example: Pt = 0 dBm, Pr(min) = −28 dBm, so budget = 28 dB. Over 80 km at 0.25 dB/km, fibre loss = 20 dB. Two connectors at 0.5 dB and four splices at 0.1 dB add 1.4 dB. With 3 dB margin, total = 24.4 dB. The link passes with 3.6 dB spare.

keyPoints: Numerical aperture is NA = √(n1² − n2²); single-mode step-index fibre needs V = 2πaNA/λ below 2.405.
Attenuation loss in dB is 10 log10(Pin/Pout); low-loss silica windows are near 850, 1300 and 1550 nm.
Modal dispersion dominates multimode fibre; chromatic and polarisation-mode dispersion remain in single-mode fibre.
LEDs suit short multimode links; semiconductor lasers suit long single-mode links; PIN and APD photodiodes detect light.
WDM carries several wavelengths on one fibre; multiplexers combine and demultiplexers separate them, and EDFAs amplify bands.
Link budget: Pt − Pr(min) must cover fibre loss × length plus connector, splice and margin losses; use datasheet values and check national standards.

en.title: Satellite communications
en.short: Orbits, transponders, earth stations, link budgets, multiple access and propagation losses.

sections.heading: Orbits and transponders
sections.text:
GEO (geostationary orbit) is about 35,786 km above the equator and appears fixed. LEO (low Earth orbit) is closer: low delay, small footprint, so a constellation is needed. MEO (medium Earth orbit) is a middle ground between LEO and GEO; HEO (highly elliptical orbit) serves high latitudes.

A transponder is the satellite repeater: it receives, shifts frequency, amplifies and retransmits. A bent-pipe transponder does not demodulate; a regenerative one does.

sections.heading: Earth stations and links
sections.text:
An earth station has an antenna, high-power amplifier (HPA), low-noise amplifier (LNA), up/down converters and a modem. EIRP is transmit power plus antenna gain, in dBW. Received carrier is C = EIRP − FSL − L + G_r, where FSL is free-space loss and L other losses. Noise is N = kTB, with k = −228.6 dBW/K/Hz.

Downlink example: EIRP = 50 dBW, f = 12 GHz, d = 38,000 km, G_r = 40 dBi, L = 2 dB, T = 150 K, B = 36 MHz.
FSL = 32.44 + 20 log10(38,000) + 20 log10(12,000) = 205.62 dB
C = 50 − 205.62 − 2 + 40 = −117.62 dBW
N = −228.6 + 10 log10(150) + 10 log10(36,000,000) = −131.28 dBW
C/N = 13.66 dB

sections.heading: Multiple access
sections.text: Multiple access shares a transponder. FDMA gives each station a frequency band; TDMA gives it a time slot; CDMA lets users share the whole band by code. Demand assignment (DAMA) allocates slots or bands as needed. Spot beams reuse frequencies.

sections.heading: Propagation impairments
sections.text: Free-space loss always applies. Rain and cloud attenuate Ku and Ka bands, causing rain fade; gaseous absorption, scintillation and depolarisation also matter. A link needs margin above the required C/N. LEO links suffer Doppler shift and frequent handover. Solar outage occurs when the Sun aligns with the earth station antenna.

keyPoints: GEO sits about 35,786 km above the equator and appears fixed; LEO gives lower delay but needs a constellation.
A transponder receives, frequency-shifts, amplifies and retransmits; a regenerative one also demodulates and remodulates.
Link budget: C = EIRP − FSL − L + G_r, with FSL = 32.44 + 20 log10(d_km) + 20 log10(f_MHz) dB.
Noise power is N = kTB, with k = −228.6 dBW/K/Hz, and C/N = C − N.
FDMA uses frequency, TDMA uses time and CDMA uses code to share a transponder.
Rain fade, atmospheric absorption, scintillation, depolarisation, Doppler and solar outage are key propagation impairments.

en.title: Mobile and wireless communications
en.short: Cellular reuse, handover, fading and diversity, multiple access, with GSM, UMTS and LTE examples.

sections.heading: Cellular reuse
sections.text: A cellular network divides an area into cells. Each cell is served by a base station. The same frequency channels are reused in cells far enough apart, because radio spectrum is scarce. A cluster is a group of cells in which every channel is used once. Its size N follows N = i² + ij + j², where i and j are non-negative integers, not both zero. The reuse distance is D = R√(3N), with R the cell radius. Larger N means weaker co-channel interference but fewer channels per cell. Example: N = 7 and R = 1 km give D = 1 × √(3 × 7) = √21 ≈ 4.58 km.

sections.heading: Handover and fading
sections.text: Handover transfers a call or data session from one cell to another as the user moves. In hard handover the old link breaks before the new one is made. In soft handover the mobile is connected to more than one base station at once, so the change is make-before-break. Fading is variation in received power. Large-scale fading comes from distance and shadowing by buildings. Small-scale multipath fading comes from many reflected waves adding at the receiver; it can be Rayleigh or Rician. Diversity reduces fading by combining independent copies of the signal in space, frequency, time or antenna polarisation.

sections.heading: Multiple access
sections.text: Multiple access lets many users share one medium. FDMA gives each user a frequency channel. TDMA gives each user a time slot. CDMA gives each user a code, and all users share the same frequency and time. OFDMA divides the band into many narrow subcarriers and assigns groups to users. GSM uses FDMA with TDMA. UMTS uses wideband CDMA. LTE uses OFDMA in the downlink and SC-FDMA in the uplink. These are examples, not a permanent ladder: later systems change the mix.

keyPoints: Cellular reuse uses the same channels in separated cells; cluster size N = i² + ij + j² and reuse distance D = R√(3N).
A larger cluster reduces co-channel interference but lowers the number of channels available in each cell.
Hard handover breaks before making the new link; soft handover makes before breaking.
Multipath fading is reduced by diversity, which combines independent copies of the signal.
FDMA, TDMA, CDMA and OFDMA share spectrum by frequency, time, code and subcarrier groups.
GSM uses FDMA with TDMA, UMTS uses wideband CDMA, and LTE uses OFDMA downlink and SC-FDMA uplink.

en.title: Microprocessors and embedded systems
en.short: CPU architecture, memory and I/O, interrupts, interfacing and embedded controllers in telecom equipment.

sections.heading: Processor architecture
sections.text: A microprocessor is a central processing unit (CPU) on one chip. It fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, executes it and writes back a result. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) does arithmetic and logic; registers hold operands and addresses; the program counter points to the next instruction; the control unit sequences operations. Address, data and control buses connect the CPU to memory and peripherals. Von Neumann designs share one bus for instructions and data; Harvard designs use separate buses. A microcontroller adds memory, timers and input/output (I/O) peripherals to a CPU core.

sections.heading: Memory and I/O
sections.text: Memory stores programs and data. RAM is volatile and loses contents when power is removed; ROM and flash keep them. Memory-mapped I/O gives a peripheral an address, so the CPU uses ordinary load and store instructions. Ports and serial links such as UART, SPI and I2C connect chips. Worked example: 16 address lines select 2¹⁶ = 65,536 addresses. With one byte per address, the space is 65,536 bytes = 64 KiB. A larger address bus gives more space: 20 lines give 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MiB.

sections.heading: Interrupts
sections.text: Polling checks a device repeatedly; interrupts let a device signal the CPU. An interrupt request (IRQ) saves the current state and jumps through a vector table to an interrupt service routine (ISR). The ISR should be short. Priority decides which interrupt wins when two arrive together; masking disables selected interrupts. Interrupt latency is the delay before the ISR runs. A watchdog timer resets a stuck controller.

sections.heading: Interfacing and controllers
sections.text: Interfacing connects the controller to sensors, radio circuits and networks. It needs correct voltage levels, drivers, isolation where necessary, and timing. Analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue converters link digital control to radio and power circuits. In telecommunications, embedded controllers supervise base-station equipment, modems, router line cards, optical modules and power alarms. They must meet real-time deadlines. Electromagnetic compatibility and safety rules differ by country, so check the local regulator and applicable standards.

keyPoints: Addressable memory = 2^n × word size, where n is the number of address lines.
A microprocessor is a CPU on a chip; a microcontroller adds memory and peripherals.
Memory-mapped I/O uses normal load and store instructions.
An interrupt saves state, runs an ISR via a vector table, then returns.
Interrupt priority and masking control competing requests; latency matters in real time.
Embedded controllers in telecom equipment must meet timing, voltage and EMC requirements.

en.title: Telecommunication network planning, management and security
en.short: Network planning and dimensioning, QoS, FCAPS management and basic security controls.

sections.heading: Planning and dimensioning
sections.text:
Planning starts with demand: how many users or devices, and when the busy hour occurs. Dimensioning turns that forecast into capacity. Add a growth margin and redundancy, then size links and equipment so busy-hour load stays below a planned utilisation.

At 120 Mbps busy-hour demand and a 70% target, required capacity is 120 ÷ 0.70 = 171.4 Mbps, so choose a 200 Mbps link. Codes and regulator rules differ by country; check current local requirements.

sections.heading: Quality of service
sections.text:
Quality of service (QoS) is the measured performance of a service. Key measures are latency (delay), jitter (delay variation), packet loss, throughput and availability. Voice needs low latency and jitter; file transfer tolerates delay but needs low loss.

QoS is enforced by classifying, marking, queuing, scheduling and shaping traffic. A service level agreement (SLA) states targets and remedies. Over-provisioning is simple but costly; priority queues are an alternative. Targets vary, so quote them from the SLA or standard in use.

sections.heading: Management functions
sections.text:
Telecom management is often described by FCAPS: fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management. Fault management detects, logs, diagnoses and clears failures. Configuration management records and controls settings, addresses and software versions, and tracks changes.

Performance management collects counters such as utilisation, error rate and delay, compares them with thresholds, and triggers upgrades. Accounting covers usage and billing; security management covers access and audit. Case: 95% utilisation and rising loss trigger a performance alarm and upgrade.

sections.heading: Security threats and controls
sections.text:
Common threats include eavesdropping, spoofing, denial of service, malware and insider misuse. Controls include authentication and access control; encryption in transit and at rest; firewalls and filtering; network segmentation; patching; logging and monitoring; and backups.

Defence in depth uses several controls because one may fail. Security is risk management: identify assets, threats and likelihood, then reduce risk to an accepted level. Legal duties and breach reporting rules are country-specific; check the national regulator and data protection law.

keyPoints: Dimensioning sizes capacity from busy-hour demand, growth margin and redundancy; required capacity = demand ÷ target utilisation.
QoS is measured by latency, jitter, packet loss, throughput and availability, and is set out in an SLA.
FCAPS covers fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management.
Fault management detects and clears failures; configuration management controls settings and changes; performance management watches counters against thresholds.
Common security threats include eavesdropping, spoofing, denial of service, malware and insider misuse.
Use defence in depth: authentication, access control, encryption, firewalls, segmentation, patching, logging and backups; check country-specific legal duties.

en.title: Professional practice, ethics and regulation
en.short: Ethics, safety, environmental duty, regulation and registration, with COREN in Nigeria as an example.

sections.heading: Ethics in engineering
sections.text:
Engineering ethics is the set of principles and rules that guide professional judgement. Its first duty is public safety, health and welfare. An engineer must be honest about data and uncertainty, work within their competence, declare conflicts of interest, keep client information confidential, and report unsafe practice. A conflict of interest is a personal or financial interest that could bias a decision.

Ethics also means refusing to overstate a design’s performance and telling a client when a cheaper option is unsafe. Codes set out these duties, but the engineer must still reason about the case.

sections.heading: Safety and environment
sections.text:
Safety in design means anticipating failure. Engineers use risk assessment to identify hazards, design margins to cover uncertainty, fail-safe defaults so a fault leaves the system safe, and current codes and standards. Codes differ by country and are revised, so check the edition that applies.

Environmental responsibility covers energy and material use, e-waste, hazardous substances and environmental impact assessment (EIA) where national law requires it. In Nigeria, EIA is part of project approval; check the exact rules with the regulator. Good practice reduces waste and plans safe disposal.

sections.heading: Regulation and registration
sections.text:
Regulation protects the public by setting entry standards and discipline. In Nigeria, COREN (the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria) is the statutory body that regulates engineering practice. It registers practitioners and enforces standards of practice and conduct. Other countries have their own bodies: the Engineering Council in the United Kingdom, state licensing boards in the United States, Engineers Canada, and ECSA in South Africa.

Registration usually requires an accredited degree, supervised experience, a professional review or examination, and continuing professional development (CPD). Details vary, so check the current rules where you will practise.

Case: Ngozi, a graduate engineer in Lagos, is asked to sign off a mast foundation without a soil report because the client is in a hurry. She should refuse, record why, and request the soil investigation. Signing would be dishonest and unsafe.

keyPoints: Engineering ethics puts public safety, health and welfare first.
COREN regulates engineering practice and registration in Nigeria; other countries have their own bodies and rules.
Registration usually requires an accredited degree, supervised experience, a professional review and continuing professional development, but details vary.
Safety is built in through risk assessment, design margins, fail-safe design and current codes and standards.
Environmental responsibility includes impact assessment, waste management and efficient use of resources.
Never sign off work you cannot verify; record and escalate pressure to do so.

en.title: Engineering project management and technical reporting
en.short: Project lifecycle, scheduling, cost, risk, teamwork, and writing and presenting a final-year report.

sections.heading: Project lifecycle and schedule
sections.text:
A project is a temporary effort to produce a defined deliverable, such as a working prototype or a final-year report. The lifecycle has phases: initiation, planning, execution, monitoring and control, and closure. Each phase ends with a milestone, a checkpoint you can verify.

Scheduling places tasks in time. A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars against a calendar. The critical path method finds the longest chain of dependent tasks; that chain sets the shortest possible project duration. Tasks not on the critical path have float, the time they can slip without delaying the project.

Example: tasks A (3 days), then B (5 days) and C (2 days), then D (4 days) after both B and C.
Paths: A-B-D = 3+5+4 = 12 days; A-C-D = 3+2+4 = 9 days.
Critical path is A-B-D, duration 12 days; C has 3 days of float.

sections.heading: Cost, risk and team
sections.text:
Cost management estimates the budget, tracks spending and controls changes. Add a contingency, a reserve for known risks. Earned value compares planned value, actual cost and earned value (the budgeted value of work completed) to judge progress.

Risk management identifies risks, assesses likelihood and impact, and plans responses: avoid, reduce, transfer or accept. A risk register lists each risk, its owner and its response.

Teamwork needs clear roles, a communication plan and regular short meetings. Record decisions so the report can show who did what.

sections.heading: Report and presentation
sections.text:
A technical report has a title, abstract, introduction, method, results, discussion, conclusion and references. Write for a busy reader: state the aim early, use headings, label figures and tables, and cite sources. Avoid copying; acknowledge help. In Nigeria, COREN regulates engineering registration, but check its current requirements; other countries have their own bodies.

For the presentation, make a few clear slides, rehearse to time, explain one key result, and prepare for questions. The final-year project is examined on both the work and how well you explain it.

keyPoints: A project lifecycle runs from initiation through planning, execution, monitoring and closure.
The critical path is the longest dependent chain; its length is the shortest project duration.
Float is the time a task can slip without delaying the project.
Cost variance = earned value − actual cost; schedule variance = earned value − planned value.
A risk register records each risk, its likelihood, impact, owner and response.
A technical report needs a clear structure and cited sources; rehearse the presentation to time.

en.title: Advanced digital communications
en.short: Advanced modulation, detection, equalisation, OFDM, channel estimation and performance bounds.

sections.heading: Modulation and detection
sections.text:
Advanced systems send several bits per symbol using M-ary modulation, such as M-QAM or M-PSK. A matched filter maximises signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant. Detection chooses the symbol with the smallest Euclidean distance to the received sample; for equal-energy signals in additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), this is maximum likelihood (ML) detection.

On a channel with memory, pulses overlap and cause intersymbol interference (ISI). The Nyquist criterion allows zero ISI when the pulse is zero at the sampling instants of the other symbols. Raised-cosine pulses trade bandwidth for smoother spectra.

sections.heading: Equalisation
sections.text: An equaliser reduces ISI. A zero-forcing equaliser inverts the channel exactly, but it amplifies noise where the channel is weak. The minimum mean-square error (MMSE) equaliser balances ISI removal against noise enhancement. Adaptive equalisers learn from training symbols; the least mean squares (LMS) algorithm updates weights in small steps to reduce error.

sections.heading: OFDM and estimation
sections.text:
Orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) splits a wideband channel into many narrow subcarriers. Each subcarrier has a long symbol time, so ISI is small. An inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) creates the time-domain symbol; a fast Fourier transform (FFT) recovers the subcarriers. A cyclic prefix copies the end of each symbol to the front; it absorbs delay spread and keeps subcarriers orthogonal if longer than the channel impulse response.

Channel estimation uses pilot symbols. Least-squares estimation divides the received pilot by the known pilot; MMSE estimation also uses noise and channel statistics. Example: 20 MHz sampling, N = 2048 subcarriers. Spacing = 20,000,000 ÷ 2048 = 9,765.625 Hz ≈ 9.77 kHz. A 144-sample prefix lasts 144 ÷ 20,000,000 = 7.2 µs and adds 144 ÷ (2048 + 144) = 6.57% overhead.

sections.heading: Performance bounds
sections.text: Performance bounds predict error rate without full simulation. For ML detection, the union bound adds pairwise error probabilities of competing symbols: P_s ≤ Σ Q(d_ij ÷ √(2N0)), where Q is the Gaussian tail probability, d_ij is symbol distance and N0 is noise power spectral density. At high SNR the minimum distance d_min dominates. These bounds guide modulation order, coding and equaliser design.

keyPoints: M-ary modulation sends log2 M bits per symbol; ML detection minimises Euclidean distance in AWGN.
The matched filter maximises SNR at the sampling instant.
Zero-forcing equalisation removes ISI but amplifies noise; MMSE equalisation balances the two.
OFDM uses IFFT/FFT and a cyclic prefix longer than the channel impulse response to keep subcarriers orthogonal.
Subcarrier spacing equals sampling rate divided by FFT size; cyclic-prefix overhead equals CP length divided by symbol length.
The union bound for ML detection is P_s ≤ Σ Q(d_ij ÷ √(2N0)), dominated by minimum distance at high SNR.

en.title: Advanced wireless communications and propagation
en.short: Stochastic channels, diversity, MIMO, beamforming, interference and cellular planning.

sections.heading: Stochastic channel models
sections.text: Radio signals arrive by many paths. A stochastic channel model treats complex gains, delays and angles as random. Rayleigh fading applies when no line of sight dominates; Rician fading adds a line-of-sight component, described by the K factor. The wide-sense stationary uncorrelated scattering (WSSUS) model is common. Delay spread sets coherence bandwidth; Doppler spread sets coherence time. These show whether the channel is flat or frequency selective, slow or fast.

sections.heading: Diversity and MIMO
sections.text: Diversity sends the same information over independent branches and combines them.
